title: {{NAME}} and the Princess Who Listened to Everything
moral: The wisest rulers are those who hear the voices others ignore.

pages.content:
Princess Sylvie had a gift that nobody knew about.

She could hear animals and fairies, not just their sounds, but their meaning. A dog's bark translated directly. A fairy's wing-song became words.

She told only {{NAME}}, her page, because he was the only person who didn't immediately try to monetise information.

"It must be useful," said {{NAME}}.

"It is," she said. "It's also very loud at breakfast. The palace ravens have very strong opinions."

pages.content:
Her first official use of the gift: a dispute between the palace bakers and a family of mice in the flour storeroom.

The bakers wanted the mice removed. The mice, as Princess Sylvie translated, were not eating the flour. They were managing a fungus that had started in the east wall and would ruin the entire supply within a month if untreated.

The bakers checked. The mice were right.

The mice stayed. The bakers gave them a dedicated shelf and a nightly portion of crumbs.

"How did you know?" the head baker asked.

"I asked," said the princess simply.

pages.content:
The fairy council came next.

They had been petitioning the palace for three years about the river toll that was damaging their reed-bed settlements. Every petition had been rejected because nobody had understood quite what they were saying.

Princess Sylvie sat with them for an afternoon and for the first time the entire council spoke and was heard.

{{NAME}} took notes.

By evening, the river toll had been restructured.

The head fairy touched the princess's hand with one tiny finger and said: "You are the first."

"I will not be the last," said the princess.

pages.content:
Her councillors were confused. The kingdom's animals seemed to know the princess by sight and regard her with unusual calm.

"It is because she hears them," {{NAME}} explained to the chief councillor.

"Hears what?"

"What they need. What they know. What they're trying to say."

The councillor looked at the princess, who was at that moment having a detailed conversation with a palace cat about the draughts in the north wing.

"She'll be the best ruler we've had in fifty years," he said slowly.

"I know," said {{NAME}}.

pages.content:
That night, returning home, {{NAME}} passed the palace gardens where birds were settling into the trees for the night.

The princess was there, sitting very still, listening to the evening chorus with her eyes closed.

He watched her for a moment: this girl surrounded by everything the kingdom had to say, patient enough to hear all of it.

He walked home thinking about what it would mean to lead that way.

In bed, he lay listening to the ordinary sounds of the street, trying to hear what they said.

Somewhere in the quiet, he thought he caught it: the world, going about its business, saying: I am here. I am here.
